It's October 2029. Mara has been singing in Jonas's choir on Thursdays for a year. Today she was late for the rehearsal because of a training course. When she arrived, the choir had already started. After the rehearsal, Jonas introduces her to a new member.
You're here at last! We'd already started without you. What happened?
The training course went on longer. And when I got to the stop, the tram had just left.
Typical. Come on, I want to introduce you to someone. This is Jakob. He plays the cello and today was his first time.
Hi, Mara. Nice to meet you. Jonas has already told me a lot about you. Before I'd even met you, I already knew you were the best nurse in Berlin.
Oh no, Jonas! What else have you told him?
Only the truth. Jakob is a primary school teacher, by the way. At the primary school on Kastanienallee.
On Kastanienallee? Then maybe you know Kuba Nowak? He's in fourth grade.
Kuba! Of course! He's in my class. Last week he handed in an essay about an old dachshund and a dog from the shelter. I had never read such a beautiful essay.
Fritz and Bruno! They're the dogs from our house. I live there on the third floor.
Then you're the Mara from the essay! The godmother who sees babies at night and rescues dogs during the day.
I didn't rescue any dog. That was Kuba. I had only set one condition.
Right, you two. I have to go home, Clara is waiting for me with the little one. Jakob, you take the M1 too, don't you? Then see Mara home.

1. Plusquamperfekt: the past of the past

When you're telling a story in the past and want to say that something had happened BEFORE another moment in the past, you use the Plusquamperfekt (like the English past perfect: “had left”, “had eaten”).
When I got to the stop, the tram had already left. (first the tram left, then I arrived)
Plusquamperfekt = Präteritum of haben / sein (hatte / war) + the participle at the end. The choice between haben and sein is exactly the same as for the Perfekt:
If you know the Perfekt, you know the Plusquamperfekt too: you just put the auxiliary in the past. “Ich habe gegessen” → “Ich hatte gegessen”. “Ich bin gegangen” → “Ich war gegangen”.
“nachdem” (after) introduces a subordinate clause (verb at the end). The action in the subordinate clause comes BEFORE the one in the main clause, so its tense is “one step further back in the past”:
After the rehearsal had finished, everyone went home.
After I passed the exam, I celebrated.
Don't confuse “nachdem” (after, conjunction, verb at the end) with “nach” (after, preposition + dative: nach der Probe) and with “danach” (afterwards, adverb, position 1).
In everyday speech Germans use the Plusquamperfekt less often; they often simply say Perfekt plus “vorher” or “schon”. But in stories, books and when the order matters, it's very useful:
Mara was tired, because she had worked all night.
He didn't know that she had already left.
We had already started without you.
I had never seen him before.
After she had eaten, she went to sleep.
After we had arrived, we called.
After he had passed the exam, he celebrated.

It was a cold October evening. When Mara and Jakob came out of the parish hall, where the choir rehearsed every Thursday, the rain had just stopped. The streets were shining in the light of the street lamps. They walked to the stop in silence, both a little embarrassed, like people who had only just met and didn't know what to talk about.

The M1 came on time. They sat down next to each other, right at the front, behind the driver. Mara always sat right at the front. She had learnt that from Ludwig, in her first year in Berlin, when he had explained to her that from there you see the city best, “like a tram driver, just without the responsibility”.
Can I ask you something? How did you actually end up in Berlin? Kuba wrote in his essay that you had never been abroad before.

That was true. Before coming to Berlin, Mara had left Romania only twice: once with her school to Budapest and once with her parents to the Black Sea, in Bulgaria. She had never been on a plane until the day she had landed in Berlin with two suitcases and three jars of honey.

She told him everything. About the letter that had come one day. About her mother, who had cried, and about her father, who had gone off to his bees. About the first night, when she hadn't slept because she had been afraid. Jakob listened without interrupting her. He had a way of listening that Mara had never come across in a man before: he looked at her while he listened, not at his phone, not out of the window, but at her.
And you? Are you from Berlin?

No. I'm from a small village in Thuringia. I moved to Berlin five years ago, after my grandmother had died. She had given me the cello when I was seven. Once she was gone, I couldn't stay in the village any more. Everything reminded me of her.

Mara looked at him. She thought of Ludwig, who after Ingrid's death hadn't played the guitar for years. Of Mrs Hoffmann, who had lost her father shortly after he had heard her for the first time at the Konzerthaus. She thought that every person she had met in Berlin carried a story they told no one, until someone asked.

Then Jakob told her about his work. He had been teaching for three years at the primary school on Kastanienallee, fourth grade, German, music and general studies. There were twenty-four children from eleven countries in his class. “Some children had only been in Germany for a few months when they came into my class,” he said. “They hadn't spoken a word of German before. A little girl from Syria had lost her books while fleeing and on the first day she only brought a pencil. Today she writes the best essays in the class. After Kuba, of course.” Mara laughed. She thought of Rana, the doctor from Syria she had met at the B1 exam. She wondered whether Rana was working as a paediatrician again by now, as she had wished.

When the tram stopped at Kastanienallee, they almost didn't notice. Mara had forgotten to pay attention to the stops. Only after the driver had rung the bell twice did she jump up. “That's my stop!” she cried. Jakob stood up too. “And mine,” he said. “The school is here.” It was half past nine. The school had been closed for hours. Mara said nothing. But she smiled.

He walked her to the front door. Under the chestnut tree in the courtyard, whose leaves had just turned yellow, they stopped. Up on the first floor, the yellow lamp was burning. On the fourth floor the window was closed, as it was already too cold, but you could still hear a piano, very softly.
Is that… is that the pianist from Kuba's essay? The one with the concert at the Konzerthaus?
Mrs Hoffmann. Yes. She's ninety-three. She plays every evening at nine. Today she's playing later. She went to the doctor yesterday and slept all day.

They stood there a while longer and listened. Then Jakob said: “I've heard you sometimes have parties in the courtyard. With music from the windows.” Mara nodded. “If you have another one,” he said, “I could bring my cello. If you'd like.” Mara said she would like that very much. Then she went in. On the stairs she met Ludwig, who was coming back with Fritz from their evening walk. He saw her face and didn't ask anything. He just smiled, very slightly, like someone who had known in advance what was going to happen.

In her flat, Mara sat down at the window, as on her first night in Berlin, three years ago. Back then she had been afraid. Back then she hadn't known anyone. Now she looked at the chestnut tree, at the yellow lamp on the first floor, at the light in Kuba's room, and listened to the piano on the fourth floor. Her phone vibrated. A message from an unknown number: “Thanks for the journey. I had forgotten how beautiful the M1 is at night. Jakob. PS: Jonas gave me your number. I hope that's OK.” Mara read the message three times. Then she replied: “It's OK. See you Thursday.” She put the phone aside and only then realised that she had been smiling the whole time.

The next morning at seven, in the bakery, Lena put her coffee in front of her and asked: “Well? How was choir rehearsal?” Mara replied: “Normal.” Lena gave her a long look. Then she said: “Mara Ionescu. I've known you for three years. You've never looked like this after a choir rehearsal.” Andrei, who was shaping pretzels behind her, laughed so hard that a pretzel fell on the floor. Fritz, who was waiting by the door for his bread rolls, was quicker than everyone else.

“So,” said Lena, leaning her hands on the counter, “what's his name?” Mara sipped her coffee, very slowly. “Jakob,” she said at last. “He's a teacher. He plays the cello. And he's read Kuba's essay.” Lena and Andrei looked at each other and nodded at the same time, like two detectives who had solved a case. “Then,” said Lena, “he's coming to the next courtyard party. With his cello.”
